## <span class="num">9.2.1</span> The Gram–Schmidt Process

In an inner product space, we can ask for bases that respect the geometry: bases whose vectors are mutually orthogonal and have unit length.

:::definition{9.2.1} Orthonormal basis
Let $V$ be an inner product space. A list $(v_1, \ldots, v_m)$ of vectors in $V$ is ***orthonormal*** if $$\langle v_i, v_j \rangle = \delta_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & i = j, \\ 0 & i \neq j. \end{cases}$$ Equivalently, $\|v_i\| = 1$ for all $i$, and $v_i \perp v_j$ for $i \neq j$. An ***orthonormal basis*** is an orthonormal list that is a basis.
:::

:::note
An orthonormal list is linearly independent: if $\sum_i c_i v_i = 0$, then $0 = \langle v_j, \sum_i c_i v_i \rangle = \sum_i c_i \langle v_j, v_i \rangle = c_j$ for each $j$. So in an $n$-dimensional space, every orthonormal list of length $n$ is an orthonormal basis.

In an orthonormal basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_n\}$, coordinates are computed by inner products: if $v = \sum x_i e_i$, then $\langle e_j, v \rangle = x_j$, so $$v = \sum_{i=1}^n \langle e_i, v \rangle\, e_i.$$ The inner product also takes a simple form: if $w = \sum y_j e_j$, then $$\langle v, w \rangle = \sum_{i,j} \ol{x_i}\, y_j \langle e_i, e_j \rangle = \sum_i \ol{x_i}\, y_i.$$ For real spaces this is $x^t y$; for complex spaces it is $x^* y$.
:::

:::theorem{9.2.2} Existence of orthonormal bases
Every finite-dimensional inner product space has an orthonormal basis.
:::

We give two proofs: one by induction, one constructive (Gram–Schmidt).

:::proof Proof 1 (Induction on dimension)
Let $\dim V = n$. If $n = 0$, the empty list is an orthonormal basis. For $n \geq 1$:

Pick any nonzero $v \in V$ and set $v_1 = v / \|v\|$, so $\|v_1\| = 1$. Let $S = \operatorname{span}(v_1)$. By the orthogonal decomposition theorem, $V = S \oplus S^\perp$, and $\dim S^\perp = n - 1$.

The restriction of $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ to $S^\perp$ is still an inner product (the defining properties are inherited by a subspace). By induction, $S^\perp$ has an orthonormal basis $\{v_2, \ldots, v_n\}$.

Then $(v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_n)$ is orthonormal, because $v_1 \perp v_i$ for $i \geq 2$ (as $v_i \in S^\perp$); being of length $n$, it is an orthonormal basis of $V$.
:::

:::proof Proof 2 (Gram–Schmidt)
Start with any basis $\{w_1, \ldots, w_n\}$ of $V$. We inductively construct orthonormal vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ such that for each $j$, $$\operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j) = \operatorname{span}(w_1, \ldots, w_j).$$

**Step 1:** Set $v_1 = w_1 / \|w_1\|$.

**Step $j$:** Suppose $v_1, \ldots, v_{j-1}$ are orthonormal and span the same subspace as $w_1, \ldots, w_{j-1}$. Define $$u_j = w_j - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \langle v_i, w_j \rangle\, v_i.$$ This subtracts from $w_j$ its components along each $v_i$: for $l < j$, $$\langle v_l, u_j \rangle = \langle v_l, w_j \rangle - \sum_{i=1}^{j-1} \langle v_i, w_j \rangle \langle v_l, v_i \rangle = \langle v_l, w_j \rangle - \langle v_l, w_j \rangle = 0.$$ Since $w_j \notin \operatorname{span}(w_1, \ldots, w_{j-1}) = \operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_{j-1})$ (linear independence), we have $u_j \neq 0$. Set $$v_j = \frac{u_j}{\|u_j\|}.$$

By construction, $v_j \perp v_i$ for $i < j$, and $\|v_j\| = 1$. The span condition holds since $v_j \in \operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_{j-1}, w_j) = \operatorname{span}(w_1, \ldots, w_j)$ and $w_j \in \operatorname{span}(v_1, \ldots, v_j)$.
:::

:::corollary{9.2.3} Isomorphism with standard space
Every $n$-dimensional real inner product space is isomorphic to $\RR^n$ with the standard inner product, as an inner product space (that is, by a linear isomorphism that preserves inner products). Similarly, every $n$-dimensional complex inner product space is isomorphic to $\CC^n$ with the standard Hermitian inner product.
:::

:::proof
Let $\{v_1, \ldots, v_n\}$ be an orthonormal basis. The coordinate map $\varphi : V \to k^n$ sending $v = \sum a_i v_i$ to $(a_1, \ldots, a_n)$ is a linear isomorphism. Moreover, for $w = \sum b_j v_j$, $$\langle v, w \rangle = \Big\langle \sum_i a_i v_i, \sum_j b_j v_j \Big\rangle = \sum_{i,j} \ol{a_i}\, b_j\, \delta_{ij} = \sum_i \ol{a_i}\, b_i,$$ which is the standard inner product of the coordinate vectors.
:::

:::note
This says that all $n$-dimensional inner product spaces over the same field are “the same.” The choice of orthonormal basis corresponds to the choice of isomorphism with the standard space. Different orthonormal bases give different coordinate systems, all equally valid.
:::

:::example{9.2.4} Gram–Schmidt in $\RR^3$
Apply Gram–Schmidt to the basis $w_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $w_2 = (1, 0, 1)$, $w_3 = (0, 1, 1)$ of $\RR^3$ with the standard inner product.

**Step 1:** $\|w_1\| = \sqrt{2}$, so $v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1, 1, 0)$.

**Step 2:** $\langle v_1, w_2 \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1 + 0 + 0) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $$u_2 = w_2 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} v_1 = (1, 0, 1) - \frac{1}{2}(1, 1, 0) = \left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, 1\right).$$ $\|u_2\|^2 = \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4} + 1 = \frac{3}{2}$, so $v_2 = \sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}\left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, 1\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(1, -1, 2)$.

**Step 3:** $\langle v_1, w_3 \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\langle v_2, w_3 \rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(0 - 1 + 2) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}$, so $$u_3 = w_3 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} v_1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} v_2 = (0, 1, 1) - \frac{1}{2}(1, 1, 0) - \frac{1}{6}(1, -1, 2) = \left(-\frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right).$$ $\|u_3\|^2 = \frac{4}{3}$, so $v_3 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left(-\frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-1, 1, 1)$.

One checks directly that $v_3 \perp v_1$ and $v_3 \perp v_2$.
:::

## <span class="num">9.2.2</span> Orthogonal Projections

The orthogonal decomposition $V = S \oplus S^\perp$ gives a canonical way to project onto $S$. It holds whenever $S$ is finite-dimensional, even if $V$ is not, and an orthonormal basis of $S$ gives an explicit formula.

:::proposition{9.2.5} Projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace
Let $V$ be an inner product space (not necessarily finite-dimensional) and $S \subseteq V$ a finite-dimensional subspace with orthonormal basis $\{e_1, \ldots, e_k\}$. Then $V = S \oplus S^\perp$, and the decomposition of $v \in V$ is $$v = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle e_i, v \rangle\, e_i + \Big(v - \sum_{i=1}^k \langle e_i, v \rangle\, e_i\Big) \in S \oplus S^\perp.$$
:::

:::proof
Let $w = \sum_{i=1}^k \langle e_i, v \rangle e_i \in S$. For each $j \leq k$, $$\langle e_j, v - w \rangle = \langle e_j, v \rangle - \sum_i \langle e_i, v \rangle \langle e_j, e_i \rangle = \langle e_j, v \rangle - \langle e_j, v \rangle = 0.$$ Hence $\langle v - w, e_j \rangle = 0$ for all $j$, and since the $e_j$ span $S$, $v - w \in S^\perp$. So $V = S + S^\perp$, and $S \cap S^\perp = \{0\}$ by positive-definiteness.
:::

:::definition{9.2.6} Orthogonal projection
Let $V$ be an inner product space and $S \subseteq V$ a subspace with $V = S \oplus S^\perp$ (for instance, $S$ finite-dimensional). The ***orthogonal projection*** onto $S$ is the map $\pi_S : V \to V$ defined by $$\pi_S(v) = v_S, \quad \text{where } v = v_S + v_{S^\perp} \text{ with } v_S \in S,\ v_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp.$$ It is linear, by uniqueness of the decomposition.
:::

:::proposition{9.2.7} Properties of orthogonal projections
Let $\pi_S : V \to V$ be the orthogonal projection onto $S$.

<!-- list:paren-roman -->

1. $\Img(\pi_S) = S$ and $\ker(\pi_S) = S^\perp$.
2. $\pi_S^2 = \pi_S$ (i.e., $\pi_S$ is idempotent).
3. $\langle \pi_S(u), v \rangle = \langle u, \pi_S(v) \rangle$ for all $u, v \in V$.
4. If $V$ is finite-dimensional, then $\pi_{S^\perp} = \id - \pi_S$.
:::

:::proof
(i) follows from the definition. (ii) If $v = v_S + v_{S^\perp}$, then $\pi_S(v) = v_S \in S$ has decomposition $v_S + 0$, so $\pi_S(\pi_S(v)) = v_S$.

(iii) Write $u = u_S + u'$ and $v = v_S + v'$ with $u', v' \in S^\perp$. Then $$\langle \pi_S(u), v \rangle = \langle u_S, v_S + v' \rangle = \langle u_S, v_S \rangle = \langle u_S + u', v_S \rangle = \langle u, \pi_S(v) \rangle.$$

(iv) We have $v = (v - \pi_S(v)) + \pi_S(v)$ with $v - \pi_S(v) \in S^\perp$ and $\pi_S(v) \in S = (S^\perp)^\perp$ (Corollary [9.1.32](/notes/math-55a/9-1-bilinear-forms-and-inner-products#corollary-9-1-32)). This is the decomposition of $v$ in $V = S^\perp \oplus (S^\perp)^\perp$, so $\pi_{S^\perp}(v) = v - \pi_S(v)$.
:::

:::note
In the language of the next section, (iii) says that $\pi_S$ is self-adjoint.
:::

:::proposition{9.2.8} Best approximation
For $v \in V$ and $S \subseteq V$ a finite-dimensional subspace, the projection $\pi_S(v)$ is the unique vector in $S$ minimizing $\|v - s\|$ over $s \in S$.
:::

:::proof
For any $s \in S$, write $$v - s = (v - \pi_S(v)) - (s - \pi_S(v)).$$ Since $v - \pi_S(v) \in S^\perp$ and $s - \pi_S(v) \in S$, these two vectors are orthogonal, and by the Pythagorean theorem $$\|v - s\|^2 = \|v - \pi_S(v)\|^2 + \|s - \pi_S(v)\|^2 \geq \|v - \pi_S(v)\|^2,$$ with equality iff $s = \pi_S(v)$.
:::

:::example{9.2.9} Fourier series
Let $V = C^\infty(S^1, \CC)$ be the space of infinitely differentiable functions $f : \RR \to \CC$ with period $1$ (functions on the circle $S^1 = \RR/\ZZ$), with $$\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^1 \ol{f(t)}\, g(t)\, dt.$$ This is a Hermitian inner product ($\langle f, f \rangle = \int_0^1 |f(t)|^2 dt > 0$ for a continuous $f \neq 0$). The functions $f_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t}$, $n \in \ZZ$, are orthonormal: $$\langle f_n, f_m \rangle = \int_0^1 e^{2\pi i (m - n) t}\, dt = \delta_{mn}.$$ They are not a basis of $V$: their span is the subspace of trigonometric polynomials. But for each $N$, Proposition [9.2.5](/notes/math-55a/9-2-orthonormal-bases#proposition-9-2-5) applies to $S_N = \operatorname{span}(f_{-N}, \ldots, f_N)$: $$\pi_{S_N}(f) = \sum_{n=-N}^{N} \langle f_n, f \rangle f_n, \qquad \langle f_n, f \rangle = \int_0^1 e^{-2\pi i n t} f(t)\, dt.$$ The numbers $\langle f_n, f \rangle$ are the Fourier coefficients of $f$, so the partial sums of the Fourier series of $f$ are orthogonal projections, and by best approximation $\pi_{S_N}(f)$ is the trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $N$ closest to $f$. Making sense of the full infinite series requires analysis (Hilbert spaces), which we do not pursue.
:::
